title: The wheat is gathered before the tares are burned
setting: On 6 December 1832, Joseph Smith was at Kirtland, Ohio, working on his revision of the Bible. His journal says he received a revelation that day explaining the parable of the wheat and the tares in Matthew 13. Sidney Rigdon wrote it down. It is not clear whether Joseph was then reviewing the New Testament or working on the Old Testament.
summary: The revelation explains the parable of the wheat and the tares. The field is the world, and the apostles were the sowers. After the apostles died, the apostate power called Babylon sowed tares that choked the wheat and drove the church into the wilderness. In the last days the blade is springing up again, but it is still tender. Angels are ready to reap, but the Lord tells them to wait so the wheat is not destroyed. At harvest the wheat will be gathered first, and then the tares will be bound and burned. It tells priesthood holders that they are lawful heirs through the lineage of their fathers. If they continue in the Lord’s goodness, they will be a light to the Gentiles and a savior to Israel.

contextNote.title: Why the order of the harvest changes
contextNote.text: In Matthew 13:30 the tares are gathered first, then the wheat. Verse 7 reverses that order: the wheat is gathered out before the tares are bound. Verse 6 gives the reason for waiting: the blade is tender, and pulling tares now would destroy wheat too. The aside in verse 6, “your faith is weak,” shows how young the restored church was. Joseph Smith’s Bible revision of Matthew 13:30 made the same change in order. In this passage, the harvest is first a gathering of the faithful, and the burning comes after.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 85–87, “Stand Ye in Holy Places,” includes this explanation of the parable. According to verse 11, what must priesthood holders do to be a light to the Gentiles and a savior to Israel?
reviewNote: Read all 11 verses. Heading gives Kirtland, 6 December 1832, while reviewing the Bible translation manuscript. JSP historical introduction gives the journal entry, Sidney Rigdon as scribe, the reversed order in the revised Matthew 13:30, and uncertainty over whether the revelation came before or after that revision. Babylon (v. 3) is figurative and not mapped. Fact-check 2026-10-12: no changes.
